newsitem.title: USA: Stock rally seen faltering, jobs data.
newsitem.headline: Stock rally seen faltering, jobs data.

text.p: Stocks are expected to run out of momentum this week with investors focusing on a Federal Reserve policy meeting and a slew of economic data ending with Friday's January employment report.

Keeping investors on edge will be the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee meeting on Tuesday and Wednesday to rule on interest rate policy. While Wall Street expects the committee to keep rates unchanged, FOMC meetings are usually cause for some apprehension among market players.

The Dow Jones industrial average finished Friday down 10.77 points, or 0.16 percent, at 6,813.09 after back-to-back sessions of gains over 80 points. Analysts attributed the decline Friday to profit-taking.
The blue-chip index finished the week up 116.6 points.
"I think we could see a week of corrections," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co.
"My guess is that the 6,900 area on the Dow will once again prove to be the height of the range," he said.
Friday's January unemployment rate and nonfarm payrolls are the week's most eagerly awaited numbers, not least because they are closely watched by the Fed.

"It's important because (Fed chairman Alan) Greenspan watches it," said Roy Blumberg, chief investment strategist at Josephthal Lyon & Ross. "No one gave a darn about the Employment Cost Index until they learned Greenspan watches it. And any Fed chairman will be watching employment data."
But he said that the effect of the data would be limited to Friday. "These numbers are good for a day's worth of action, unless they are unbelievably off expectations," he said.
Blumberg said he doubted the FOMC would take any action on interest rates.
"But with every meeting the odds increase that it will raise rates at the next one," he added. "The economy is a bit stronger than expected."

On Friday the government reported the nation's gross domestic product expanded at a robust 4.7 percent annual rate in the fourth quarter. The GDP number was above Wall Street economists' expectations of a 3.9 percent annual rate.
Not all analysts, however, agreed the market would move lower this week.
Hildegard Zagorski, an analyst at Prudential Securities, said she expected stocks to move higher with occasional shakeouts.
Phil Orlando, chief investment strategist of Value Line's Asset Management division, said last week's round of data has given the market a positive tone.
"What changed last week is that we got data that confirmed that the moderate growth and benign inflation thesis is accurate," Orlando said.
Other data this week include the January National Association of Purchasing Management Index due on Monday, and December new home sales and leading indicators due on Tuesday.
